problem.text: Suppose that real number $x$ satisfies $$\sqrt{49-x^2}-\sqrt{25-x^2}=3.$$ What is the value of $\sqrt{49-x^2}+\sqrt{25-x^2}$?

steps.title: Where to start: give the two roots names
steps.body: We are told the difference of two square roots and asked for their sum. A difference times a sum is a difference of squares, and squaring a square root removes the root. So let $a = \sqrt{49-x^2}$ and $b = \sqrt{25-x^2}$, and look at $a^2$ and $b^2$.

your_turn.answer: $(49 - x^2) - (25 - x^2) = 24$. The $x^2$ cancels, so it is $24$ for every $x$.

steps.title: Careful: do not plug in $x = 0$
steps.body: It is tempting to try $x = 0$, since it makes both roots whole numbers. But the answer has to come from an $x$ that satisfies the given equation, so test it first.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
Factor the difference of squares and use $a - b = 3$:
$$24 = a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b) = 3(a+b).$$
So $a + b = 8$. Such an $x$ really exists: $a = 5.5$ and $b = 2.5$ give $x^2 = 18.75$ in both roots. The answer is **(A)** $8$.

wrong_choices.E: This comes from plugging in $x = 0$ to get $7 + 5 = 12$. But $x = 0$ gives a difference of $7 - 5 = 2$, not $3$, so it does not satisfy the equation.
